hero.subtitle: Copper Tripeptide-3 · Research Formulation
hero.shortDescription: AHK-Cu Spray is a Veracue Research Use Only product built around AHK-Cu, the copper(II) complex of the tripeptide L-alanyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine (Ala-His-Lys), listed by many ingredient suppliers as Copper Tripeptide-3. The most directly relevant published study (Pyo et al., 2007) tested AHK-Cu on isolated human scalp hair follicles and cultured human dermal papilla cells — ex vivo and in vitro evidence only. No human clinical trial of AHK-Cu was identified, so this material does not establish hair growth, treatment effect or safety in people.

sections.heading: What Is AHK-Cu?
paragraphs: AHK-Cu is the copper(II) complex of the tripeptide L-alanyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine, written Ala-His-Lys or A-H-K. Ingredient suppliers commonly list it as Copper Tripeptide-3, distinct from Copper Tripeptide-1, the trade name used for GHK-Cu.

The name itself describes the chemistry: three amino acids, alanine, histidine and lysine, joined into a short peptide chain that binds a copper(II) ion. That single-amino-acid difference from GHK-Cu, alanine in place of glycine at the first position, is enough to make AHK-Cu a distinct chemical entity. Its own published evidence base is, in turn, much smaller.

AHK-Cu Spray is a Veracue Research Use Only product named around AHK-Cu. The molecule and the finished product are not the same thing. AHK-Cu has a defined chemical identity and a small published literature. The Veracue formulation, including its concentration, vehicle and other properties, is set by that product's own documentation, not by the molecule's literature.

Sources also report more than one molecular weight for AHK-Cu. That happens because they describe different forms of the same compound: the free peptide, the neutral copper complex, or a hydrochloride salt. The reference values below are for the compound itself, not a claim about the Veracue formulation.

sections.heading: AHK-Cu vs GHK-Cu
paragraphs: AHK-Cu and GHK-Cu are different compounds. Both are copper(II) complexes of a tripeptide ending in histidine-lysine, but AHK-Cu starts with alanine while GHK-Cu starts with glycine.

GHK-Cu was first identified in human plasma and carries a much larger research literature. AHK-Cu's direct evidence centres on a single 2007 study. No head-to-head comparison of the two was identified. Findings reported for GHK-Cu should not be applied to AHK-Cu, and neither compound can be called stronger on the strength of the other's literature.

sections.heading: Reading AHK-Cu Research Accurately
paragraphs: Online material about AHK-Cu often blends three different things. It mixes findings about GHK-Cu, marketing claims from consumer AHK-Cu scalp serums, and the narrow ex vivo and in vitro evidence base for AHK-Cu itself. For research purposes, it helps to keep these separate.

Consumer AHK-Cu hair serums and scalp sprays are formulated cosmetic products, positioned and evaluated on different terms than a laboratory research material. Veracue AHK-Cu Spray is not compared with, or evaluated against, those products. Marketing claims made for consumer formulations do not transfer to this Research Use Only material.

When a source discusses AHK-Cu, it is worth checking whether it is citing the Pyo et al. (2007) study, the primary direct evidence, or restating claims that actually trace back to GHK-Cu research instead. The comparison in the section above exists so that distinction is easy to make.

sections.heading: Intended Research Applications
paragraphs: AHK-Cu Spray is offered for in vitro and laboratory research: for example, cell-culture and tissue-culture work in hair-follicle and dermal papilla biology, copper-peptide chemistry, or analytical method development. It is not a drug, cosmetic, supplement or food, and it is not intended for administration to humans or animals.
Research-use positioning is not only a label. Nothing on this page provides, or should be read as, dosing, application, reconstitution-for-administration or treatment information.

sections.heading: What the Published Research Investigated
paragraphs: The primary direct evidence reviewed here is from ex vivo human hair follicles and in vitro dermal papilla cells. It comes from a single study led by a dermatology group at Seoul National University (Pyo et al., 2007). That study added AHK-Cu to culture medium in two linked experiments.

Isolated human scalp hair follicles were maintained in organ culture for 12 days, 240 follicles from three donors, and exposed to AHK-Cu across a concentration range. Cultured human dermal papilla cells, the specialised fibroblasts at the follicle base, were tested separately for proliferation and markers of apoptosis.

evidenceTable.heading: Research Evidence Summary
rows: Ex vivo human hair follicle organ culture
Follicle elongation increased at 10⁻¹² to 10⁻⁹ M compared with vehicle
In vitro human dermal papilla cells
Proliferation increased at 10⁻¹² to 10⁻⁹ M; at 10⁻⁹ M the Bcl-2/Bax ratio rose and cleaved caspase-3 and PARP fell, alongside a reduction in apoptotic cells that was not statistically significant
No animal study was identified in the literature reviewed for this page
No human clinical trial was identified in the literature reviewed for this page

sections.closing: These findings describe AHK-Cu added directly to culture medium, not a finished spray product. They also have not been independently replicated in the sources reviewed for this page. Ex vivo and in vitro results indicate biological activity worth further study. On their own, they do not establish an effect in living people.
sections.extraParagraph: Evidence about AHK-Cu the molecule is also not the same as evidence about a specific finished product. The 2007 study describes AHK-Cu dissolved directly in laboratory culture medium; it does not describe delivery through a spray device, a vehicle or human skin. Confirming that a formulation delivers AHK-Cu at a given concentration, or that it behaves the same way the molecule did in culture, requires dedicated formulation testing. That testing is not part of the current documentation. The study authors proposed that AHK-Cu promotes hair follicle growth through its effects on dermal papilla cell proliferation and apoptosis. That proposal is a mechanistic hypothesis put forward by the researchers, not a demonstrated clinical outcome.

sections.heading: AHK-Cu Spray Formulation Transparency
paragraphs: Veracue publishes what it has confirmed about this product and is direct about what it has not yet published. The fields below reflect the current state of Veracue's public product information for AHK-Cu Spray.

A spray format describes how a product is packaged and dispensed. On its own, it does not specify the compound's concentration, the vehicle it is dissolved in, or the route the packaging was designed for. Those specifics belong in the product's own documentation, once published, not in general AHK-Cu literature.

Publishing these fields once they are confirmed benefits researchers directly: a stated concentration and vehicle let a study be designed and reported accurately, and a stated pH and salt form let a reader judge whether findings from one lot are likely to generalise to another.

sections.closing: For copper-peptide formulations, pH and the peptide-to-copper ratio can affect which chemical form is present in solution. That is one reason formulation details belong in the product's own documentation rather than in general AHK-Cu literature.

sections.heading: Research Use Only
paragraphs: AHK-Cu Spray is supplied for laboratory research use only. It is not a cosmetic, hair-care, therapeutic or consumer product. It is not intended for human or veterinary use, and it is not intended for ingestion, injection or any form of administration. It has not been evaluated by the FDA.

Veracue does not provide human dosage, spray counts, frequency or application instructions for this product, and none should be inferred from the AHK-Cu literature discussed above. Researchers should follow their own approved laboratory procedures and this product's documentation. Contact our team if a protocol requires formulation information the current documentation does not include.
Store and handle the product according to the conditions stated in its own documentation and label. Handle it as a laboratory chemical, using appropriate personal protective equipment.

faq.answer: AHK-Cu Spray is a Veracue Research Use Only product named around AHK-Cu, the copper(II) complex of the tripeptide Ala-His-Lys. It is supplied for laboratory research, and product-specific formulation details should be taken from current first-party documentation.

faq.question: What is AHK-Cu?
faq.answer: AHK-Cu is the copper(II) complex of L-alanyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine. It is commonly listed by ingredient suppliers as Copper Tripeptide-3.

faq.question: Is AHK-Cu the same as GHK-Cu?
faq.answer: No. AHK-Cu starts with alanine and GHK-Cu starts with glycine. They are different compounds, and GHK-Cu's much larger literature should not be applied to AHK-Cu.

faq.question: What did the published AHK-Cu research actually investigate?
faq.answer: The primary direct evidence is a 2007 study that added AHK-Cu to culture medium bathing isolated human hair follicles and cultured human dermal papilla cells. It is ex vivo and in vitro evidence.

faq.question: What did the AHK-Cu hair follicle research find?
faq.answer: Isolated human scalp hair follicles, cultured for 12 days, showed increased elongation at AHK-Cu concentrations of 10⁻¹² to 10⁻⁹ M compared with vehicle.

faq.question: What did the AHK-Cu dermal papilla cell research find?
faq.answer: Cultured human dermal papilla cells showed increased proliferation over the same concentration range. At 10⁻⁹ M, apoptosis-related markers also shifted, though the drop in apoptotic cell count was not statistically significant.

faq.question: Are there animal studies of AHK-Cu?
faq.answer: No animal study was identified in the literature reviewed for this page.

faq.question: Are there human clinical trials of AHK-Cu?
faq.answer: No human clinical trial was identified in the literature reviewed for this page. The available evidence is ex vivo and in vitro.

faq.question: Is AHK-Cu proven to grow hair?
faq.answer: No. The ex vivo and in vitro findings described above indicate biological activity worth further study. On their own, they do not establish hair growth, treatment effect or safety in people.

faq.question: What ingredients or concentration are in Veracue AHK-Cu Spray?
faq.answer: Route, form, concentration, vehicle, pH, excipients and related formulation details are not publicly specified in Veracue's current product information. They should be confirmed against first-party documentation and lot records.

faq.question: Is a certificate of analysis available for AHK-Cu Spray?
faq.answer: COA availability for this product should be confirmed with Veracue. A useful COA states identity, concentration or assay, purity method, lot number, testing date and storage conditions.

faq.question: What does AHK-Cu purity mean, and how is it different from concentration?
faq.answer: Purity describes the share of a detected signal that belongs to the AHK-Cu peak under stated test conditions. Concentration, or assay, describes how much AHK-Cu the finished product actually contains; the two are not interchangeable.

faq.question: Does Veracue provide dosage or application instructions for AHK-Cu Spray?
faq.answer: No. Veracue does not provide human dosage, spray counts or application instructions for this Research Use Only product.

faq.question: What does Research Use Only mean for AHK-Cu Spray?
faq.answer: It means the product is supplied for laboratory research only and is not a cosmetic or therapeutic product. It is also not for human or veterinary use, and it is not intended for any form of administration.
